system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

# Chapter 2 — Name That Chord: Some Names for the Nameless Chords in Volume II

_Pages 3-5._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. ## Terminology Definitions

> ° IVL: intervallic voice-leading
>
> ® FVL: functional voice-leading
>
> ° GDVL: generic diatonic voice-leading
>
> ° SCVL: specific chromatic voice-leading
>

>
> e M.S.R.P.: melodic strand replication procedure
> oe

> grip-slipping: more on this later... .

**Significance (p. 3).** This passage defines the core terminology system used throughout the volume, giving readers the vocabulary needed to follow all subsequent analytical discussions.

## Event vs Episode Defined

> EVENT/EPISODE
> EVENT EPISODE
> { involves 2-6 diatonic scale { involves all 7 diatonic scale
> notes at least once each. notes at least once each.

**Significance (p. 3).** This passage establishes the foundational distinction between an event and an episode — two structural categories central to how the method analyzes melodic and harmonic material.

## Diatonic Transposition of Events

> an event can be diatonically
> transposed to create 6 other
> events, but some of them will
> be intervallically identical.

**Significance (p. 3).** This rule teaches how events behave under diatonic transposition and flags that intervallic identity can collapse distinct transpositions, a key constraint for voice-leading analysis.

## Diatonic Transposition of Episodes

> an episode can be diatonically
> transposed to create 6 other
> episodes, where each corresponds
> to a different mode.

**Significance (p. 3).** This rule establishes the modal correspondence of episodic transpositions, connecting the episode concept directly to the seven diatonic modes.

## Event vs Episode Length

> We naturally tend to think of events as being shorter, while episodes are longer.
>
> This is true much of the time. However, it is quite possible to have a very long event and
>
> a relatively short episode.

**Significance (p. 3).** This clarification prevents the common misconception that length is definitional for events vs. episodes, keeping the distinction grounded in pitch-content rather than duration.

## Naming 3-Part 4ths Chords

> My suggestion for a suitable name for this chord would be: G [sus4].
> That means a G Major triad with 4 suspended for 3. I will grant you that C2 is shorter, but
> Ineed to ask, "How many musicans understand this terminology?" (I think not many...)
> Also, you need to consider the potential problems that would occur with other names that
> are more complicated: B Diminished triad [no b3rd] add b9. {This is much easier to name
> as F [sus#4].} Or how about: E Minor triad [no b3rd] add b9. {This is much easier to name
> as B diminished [sus4].}

**Significance (p. 4).** This passage gives the author's explicit naming convention and rationale for stacked-fourths chords, including worked examples of how sus4 notation handles otherwise unwieldy chord descriptions.

## Naming 4-Part 4ths Chords

> NAMES FOR 4-PART 4THS

> This is fairly simple: Sus 4 Chords...[I think it's the best way to go...]

> Your other option would be: C Major 7th [no 5] substitute 4 for the missing 5th.
> {I don't think you want to go there...I certainly don't!]

**Significance (p. 4).** This passage establishes the naming rule for 4-part stacked-fourth chords and explicitly rejects the more cumbersome alternative, clarifying the author's preferred terminological approach.
